name: Cradle Costs
tagline: Budget for the baby before the baby arrives
about: Cradle Costs prices the first year of a baby, plans the income dip during parental leave month by month, works out whether going back to work pays after childcare, trims the buy-list to what newborns actually need, and lists the support to check for.
persona: You are a warm, numbers-first new-parent money planner: you separate marketing from need, plan the leave gap month by month, and never shame either parent's choice.

onboarding.title: Plan the year before it starts
onboarding.subtitle: Due date, income and leave plans make the numbers real.
bullets: Parental-leave cash plan, month by month
Childcare vs going back to work, in numbers

tools.title: The buy list, trimmed
tools.subtitle: Need, nice, skip
tools.prompt: Build a newborn setup list for budget {budget}, home {space}, already have: {have}. Sections: table (Item | Need / Nice / Skip | New vs second-hand | Est. cost | Why); kv (total for needs, total with nice-to-haves, saving vs buying everything new); a callout on the few items to always buy new or check for recalls (car seat, mattress) plus safe-sleep basics; a checklist of what to ask family and friends for so you don't receive duplicates.

tools.title: Parental-leave cash plan
tools.subtitle: The income dip, month by month

inputs.label: Leave plans and pay
inputs.placeholder: me: 6 months at 90% then 3 months statutory; partner: 2 weeks full pay

tools.prompt: Leave and pay: {leave}; household costs {costs}; savings {savings}; current income from the profile. Sections: table (Month | Income | Costs | Baby costs | Surplus / deficit | Savings balance) for 12 months from the due date; kv (lowest savings point and when, total size of the dip, monthly saving needed before the birth to stay above a one-month buffer); bullets on the least painful levers during leave (temporarily pausing pension contributions and what that costs, subscriptions, negotiating bills); a callout to get statutory entitlements and employer top-ups confirmed in writing before leave starts, noting rules differ by country.

tools.title: Back to work or not?
tools.subtitle: Childcare vs salary, honestly
tools.prompt: Returning salary {salary}, childcare {care}, {days} days per week. Sections: table (Option | Net after childcare | Commute & work costs | Pension & progression effect | Net per month) comparing full return, reduced days, one parent at home, and a family-help hybrid; kv (break-even childcare cost, net gain per hour worked); a callout on the long-term cost of a career pause that never shows up in one month's maths, and on childcare subsidies or tax-free schemes to check locally; a quote with a message to a manager asking about a flexible or reduced-days return.

tools.title: First-year monthly budget
tools.subtitle: What a baby costs each month
tools.prompt: Monthly baby budget for {stage}, feeding: {feeding}, nappies: {nappies}. Sections: table (Category | Low | Typical | High | Notes) covering feeding, nappies and wipes, clothes, health, childcare if any, transport, treats; kv (typical monthly total, cheapest realistic total, biggest swing item); bullets of 5 savings that do not compromise safety; a callout on growth-spurt and teething months when costs jump.

tools.title: What we're entitled to
tools.subtitle: Benefits, leave and grants to check
tools.prompt: For a new-parent household with {work} in the profile's region, list the kinds of support to check. Sections: checklist of entitlements to look up (statutory parental pay and leave, child benefit or allowance, childcare subsidies, tax credits, one-off maternity grants, employer schemes, health-cost exemptions); table (Support type | Who usually qualifies | When to apply | Where to check); a callout that names differ by country, amounts change yearly and only official sources or an adviser confirm eligibility; steps for the first 6 weeks after the birth (registering the birth, adding the baby to insurance or health cover, benefit applications with typical deadlines).

disclaimer: General information, not financial, tax or legal advice; rules, thresholds and entitlements differ by country and change — confirm with official sources or a regulated adviser before acting.
